ENV 3300.d: This course investigates the fundamentals of ecological restoration. Topics addressed include hydrologic data sources, statistical analysis in hydrologic problem-solving, snow and snowmelt, hydrograph analysis, hydrographic routing, hydrologic modeling and current challenges of urban hydrology, hydrologic models and hydrologic design. Use of spreadsheet software is required.

Verification burden is moderate rather than severe: misreading a statute in a classroom case study carries lower stakes than a live regulatory filing, so the dampening effect that protects higher-stakes courses does not apply as strongly here. At 24 months, actual deployment of AI into professional environmental-policy analysis is still uneven, holding the base rating at Medium.

By 2031, AI systems will plausibly draft competent statutory summaries, compliance analyses, and policy memos of the kind this course teaches, consistent with productivity research showing large time savings and quality gains on professional writing tasks. Diffusion of these tools into environmental-planning and consulting workflows will likely be well underway, though still uneven per Census BTOS adoption data. No licensure, accreditation floor, or foundational role protects this elective from that erosion — it is not gatekeeping later required coursework and carries no professional credentialing mandate. As base automatability of statutory analysis and policy writing rises with capability and adoption together, the instrumental case for a student personally producing this analysis weakens substantially, pushing the rating to High even as classroom judgment about case studies retains some value.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems performing most routine statutory interpretation and policy-analysis drafting competently, consistent with the rapid capability trend documented in task-time-horizon research on doubling AI capability. Because the course has neither an institutional lock-in nor a scaffolding role for later required coursework, nothing in the rating structure caps that erosion, and the rating remains High. The genuine uncertainty is not whether AI can produce plausible-sounding policy analysis by 2036 — it very likely can — but how much contested, high-stakes environmental-policy judgment still requires a human who understands the underlying statutory and scientific tradeoffs well enough to catch a subtly wrong AI-generated compliance conclusion, a question this rating does not resolve with confidence at this horizon.
ENV 4200.d: This course provides an overview of environmental policy and major environmental laws in the U.S. The major statutes are analyzed in terms of purpose, scope, implementation, compliance requirements, and impact on land use. Case studies are examined in a planning context.

That verification burden pulls the rating down one band from where raw GIS-task exposure would place it, landing at Medium as these tools diffuse further into ecological-management and regulatory workflows over the horizon.

A decade out, AI-embedded geospatial platforms will plausibly execute most of the routine spatial-pattern analysis this course teaches as manual skill, under the general trend of rapidly improving AI task capability and compute growth. The instrumental case for personally performing that computation weakens substantially. What persists is the need for someone who can judge whether a landscape-ecology model's spatial interpretation is ecologically sound before it informs a real management or regulatory decision — a verification role that does not shrink merely because the underlying computation becomes automated. The rating holds Medium, capped by that structural need for expert interpretation; the uncertainty is in how much routine geospatial execution automates around that still-necessary ecological judgment, not in whether the judgment itself remains valuable.
ENV 4400.d: Students will examine the effects of spatial pattern and scale on ecological processes and learn how the concepts of landscape ecology apply to environmental policy, management, regulation, and assessment. Students will develop skills for geospatial analysis of data using various geospatial tools.

ENV 4410.d: This course surveys U.S. water law and administration. Topics include (1) why we need laws regulating water use, (2) how ancient water laws influenced U.S. water law, (3) variations of surface and groundwater law, including prior appropriation, riparian, and hybrid, (4) international and interstate agreements, and (5) a special focus on water administration in the West.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly handle more of the descriptive wetlands content and even assist with preliminary spatial classification of wetland types, consistent with observed-usage data on AI's strength in synthesis and explanatory tasks. The protective factor is that actual wetland regulatory determinations — used in permitting, mitigation, and enforcement — are contested and consequential, and an undetected misclassification is exactly the non-obvious-failure condition that keeps a knowledgeable human in the verification loop, echoing the jagged-frontier finding on misplaced trust in AI outputs outside their reliable range. That verification burden pulls the rating down one band from raw content exposure, landing at Medium as these tools diffuse into environmental-consulting workflows.

A decade out, AI systems will likely generate fluent wetland-ecosystem explanations and assist substantially with spatial classification, under the general trend of rapidly improving AI task capability and continued compute growth. The instrumental case for a student learning this material purely as informational content weakens considerably. What persists is the need for someone who can make and defend a contested wetland-boundary or impact determination that will hold up under regulatory or legal scrutiny — a verification and judgment role that does not shrink simply because descriptive content generation becomes automated. The rating holds Medium, capped by that structural verification need; the uncertainty concerns how much descriptive teaching content automates around that still-necessary regulatory judgment, not whether the judgment itself remains valuable.
ENV 4420.d: In this course, students learn about a broad overview of wetland landscapes. Topics include spatial distribution of wetlands (local and national), variations in wetlands topology (salt-water versus fresh-water and warmer versus colder climates), relationships between wetlands (migratory flight paths), wetlands ecosystems, human impacts on wetlands, federal, state, and local wetlands regulations, and international wetlands problems.

r: Habitat Planning applies conservation-biology principles to urban expansion, recreation, transportation, and energy-development pressures on wildlife habitat, producing planning solutions analyzed across multiple spatial and political scales. Verification burden and embodiment are only moderate protective factors here: much of the analytical work is desk-based and the stakes, while real, are typically reviewed by agencies rather than immediately safety-critical, so the dampener protecting field-embodied courses does not apply. Ten years out, the capability trend — task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months per METR/Epoch analysis — makes it plausible that AI systems competently produce full habitat-conservation plans, spatial trade-off analyses, and policy documents with limited human drafting. Still, absent any accreditation or licensure floor and with the course positioned as a terminal upper-division elective rather than prerequisite substrate, no structural factor caps the rating downward. The wide-uncertainty caveat is genuine: this is a confident-direction, not a confident-point, forecast. Rating remains High, contingent on continued diffusion of planning-specific AI tools into conservation practice.
ENV 4430.d: This is an interdisciplinary course designed to examine the forces and impacts of urban expansion and other human activities (e.g., recreation, transportation, energy development) on ecological processes and wildlife habitats. Topics include conservation biology principles, problems with wildlife habitat conservation, and planning solutions to preserve wildlife habitat. Multiple spatial and political scales provide the context for analysis.

r: Lake and River Systems trains students to examine the physical, chemical, and biological components of lakes, reservoirs, ponds, and riparian ecosystems, investigating how water balance, nutrient loading, and pollution inputs shape ecological and water-quality outcomes. Diffusion of environmental-monitoring AI into limnological practice will likely be uneven, consistent with Census BTOS evidence that AI adoption lags capability broadly. The dampener from low embodiment and low verification tolerance holds the rating down despite rising raw capability. Some routine data-crunching offloads to AI, but the field-based core of the course is not substituted.

ENV 4440.d: Students in this course examine the study of lakes, reservoirs, and ponds as inland water ecosystems, as well as rivers and riparian ecosystems. The physical, chemical, and biological components of surface waters are examined. Students investigate how these systems are formed and how they evolve over time. The shape of the system, its water balance, and the nutrient and pollution inputs are studied with respect to their influence on ecology and surface water health. Students learn how the physical, chemical, and biological factors in these ecosystems affect water quality.

ENV 4450.d: This course explores the diversity of running water ecosystems throughout the world by examining the chemistry, physical features, and biology of stream ecosystems. Principles of stream ecology will be used to examine local stream ecosystems ranging from those found in the mountains to the prairies. The relationship among a stream, its watershed, floodplain, and riparian zone will be studied. Human activities that alter water quality, chemistry, and the ecology of a stream will be investigated, as well as methods to mitigate and protect lotic (flowing water) ecosystems.

ENV 4460.d: This course examines the interplay between humans, our activities, and water quality. Topics include nutrient cycling, water and wastewater treatment, chemical and biological contamination, and hydraulics. This course uses problem based learning through modeling to examine water quality using real world examples and mass balance evaluations. Field trips to water and wastewater treatment plants are required.

ENV 4470.d: In this course, students focus on snow processes and their function as part of the hydrologic cycle. Topics include snow formation in the atmosphere, snow accumulation and measurement, snow distribution, snowpack metamorphism and basic energy exchange principles, snow chemistry, snow ablation and runoff, watershed processes, and snow management issues. Course content is amplified through case studies and/or field trip(s).
